This paper presents an eight-step MBSE approach for defining the behaviors of the CubeSats. The approach begins with a well-defined set of mission requirements and ends with a representation of the functional architecture captured as an activity hierarchy.

bibliographic_review_management.citation: Kaslow, D., Ayres, B., Cahill, P. T., Hart, L., and Yntema, R. (2017). A Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) Approach for Defining the Behaviors of CubeSats. 2017 IEEE Aerospace Conference.
bibliographic_review_management.title: A Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) Approach for Defining the Behaviors of CubeSats

RQ1.rationale: The paper provides a generalized CubeSat mission-behavior modeling method, but it does not model EPS and does not explicitly frame the method as requiring minimal prior behavioral knowledge.

RQ2.rationale: It claims system-level MBSE benefits such as reduced development risk, improved quality, traceability, generalizability, and single-source-of-truth, but these are not EPS-specific and are not empirically demonstrated.

RQ3.rationale: Verification is mentioned only as general MBSE scope or future work; no EPS model or pre-physical-development EPS verification procedure is integrated.

bibliographic_review_management.lineage_overlap_notes: The work explicitly complements the INCOSE SSWG CubeSat Reference Model and uses examples from that model; potential lineage overlap with cited earlier CubeSat MBSE reference-model and RAX work was noted but not consulted.

RQ1: A generalized eight-step SysML/MBSE workflow models CubeSat mission behavior from mission requirements to use cases, scenarios, activities, and an activity hierarchy/functional architecture.
The approach uses generic Collect Mission Data and Distribute Mission Data requirements that teams can tailor to unique missions.

It handles behavior definition through top-down refinement rather than requiring a full detailed behavior model upfront, but it does not explicitly discuss minimal behavioral knowledge and does not address EPS.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include single-source-of-truth, enhanced communication, reduced development risk, improved quality, knowledge transfer, traceability, recursive reuse, and generalizability.
Evidence for outcomes is mostly author argument and illustrative SysML artifacts; there are no EPS-specific reliability, reproducibility, or integrability metrics.
RQ3: No EPS verification procedure is modeled or integrated before physical development.
Verification of functional requirements is named as future work, not a demonstrated part of the method.
